theme.story: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 50, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Binary search halves the search space on every comparison: compute mid, compare, discard one half, repeat. The run is bounded by O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

theme.title: The obsidian vault of the sunken vault corridor — Sealed
theme.story: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 0, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: A write pointer plus a read pointer relocates non-zero values in one pass, in O(1) extra space. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

title: Move zeroes to the end
topic: arrays
learningObjective: A write pointer plus a read pointer relocates non-zero values in one pass, in O(1) extra space.

complexity: time O(n), space O(1)

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Stack, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Pushing every opener and popping on each closer makes mismatches obvious at the top of the stack. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Hash Table, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Counting with a hash map trades space for time: one pass records every frequency, and the largest count is the answer. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Trees, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 88, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The ways to reach step i reuse smaller answers: step 1 or 2 at a time means ways[i] is the sum of the two previous counts. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

theme.story: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 3 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n × n!) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Each open position tries every unused value: mark it used, fill the rest, then free it — freeing is what lets the next branch reuse the value. The run is bounded by O(n × n!) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

problem.canonicalAlgorithm: Track reach=0. For each index i in order, if i is beyond reach the end is unreachable; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i+jumps[i]). Reaching the last index wins.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Binary search halves the search space on every comparison: compute mid, compare, discard one half, repeat. The run is bounded by O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 50, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 50, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(log n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Binary search halves the search space on every comparison: compute mid, compare, discard one half, repeat. The run is bounded by O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Arrays, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 0, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Two values that are the wrong way round cannot both be where they are. Exchanging them puts both right in a single move.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: A write pointer plus a read pointer relocates non-zero values in one pass, in O(1) extra space. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Stack, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A stack hands values back in the opposite order to the one they went in. Adding to it only ever touches the top.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Add to the top, never into the middle. A stack has no middle to add to.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Pushing every opener and popping on each closer makes mismatches obvious at the top of the stack. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Hash Table, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Counting with a hash map trades space for time: one pass records every frequency, and the largest count is the answer. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Trees, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 5 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 88, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Dynamic Programming, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 6 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n) in the worst case, O(1) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: The ways to reach step i reuse smaller answers: step 1 or 2 at a time means ways[i] is the sum of the two previous counts. The run is bounded by O(n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

theme.story: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Backtracking, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 3 lanterns. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A named value is how the program remembers something without carrying it around. It is the cheapest kind of storage there is.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Write it down in one place, and read it from there rather than working it out again.
Commit only once the rule has actually been satisfied — not when it merely feels right.
narration.win: The obsidian vault gives. Every lantern in the sunken vault corridor was handled in the order the plan demanded — O(n × n!) in the worst case, O(n) of extra space, and not one step spent that the algorithm did not require.
narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.
correctFlavour: One down in the sunken vault corridor.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Each open position tries every unused value: mark it used, fill the rest, then free it — freeing is what lets the next branch reuse the value. The run is bounded by O(n × n!) time and O(n) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

problem.canonicalAlgorithm: Track reach=0. For each index i in order, if i is beyond reach the end is unreachable; otherwise extend reach to max(reach, i+jumps[i]). Reaching the last index wins.

narration.lose: The obsidian vault stays shut. The sunken vault corridor resets, but the lanterns are exactly where you left them, and so is the plan. Same rules, different order.

debrief.summary: You worked the sunken vault corridor one lantern at a time until the obsidian vault resolved. What this problem is built to teach: Binary search halves the search space on every comparison: compute mid, compare, discard one half, repeat. The run is bounded by O(log n) time and O(1) extra space, and that bound comes from the algorithm rather than from how carefully you played.

narration.intro: A band of lanterns has been laid out along the sunken vault corridor, and only one of them opens the obsidian vault. The trap resets itself the moment you touch it in the wrong order, so work strictly in order and never guess. This is Binary Search, and it has to be done by the book. Right now the sunken vault corridor holds 8 lanterns. The obsidian vault reads 50, and it is in there somewhere. Work one at a time; the hints spell out the plan if you want them.
hintPool: Everything in the sunken vault corridor is in order, so order is the tool here. You never need to look at every value to make progress.
A comparison here does not just answer yes or no — it produces a direction, and the direction is what decides everything after it.
Whatever is left is still in order, so a whole side of it can be ruled out at once. Being able to do that is the only reason this is quick.
Finishing is a result, not a guess. The program stops when the rule allows it to stop, and reports what it found.
Do not begin at either end. Begin at the value in the middle of what is left, because that is the one that rules out the most.
Hold your lantern next to the obsidian vault and ask which is bigger. Whichever side is bigger, the other side is finished.
